strengths: Thorough empirical SVD analysis of last-layer effective rank across six diverse ViT architectures (ViT-Tiny/Large/Huge, CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, Swin-Small), with consistent methodology (99th-percentile rank across 1000 validation images) and full appendix reproductions per architecture, giving good evidence for the general claim of last-layer low-rank structure in ViTs.

The paper identifies a real and practically important phenomenon: naive feature-map MSE distillation is weak for ViTs (74.86%→75.07%), and matching the student's last-layer width to the teacher's (via a lightweight linear projector kept at inference, or by widening only the last block) substantially and consistently improves both distillation (up to 78.23%) and standalone training (up to 75.54%) for a DeiT-Tiny student.

Extensive, carefully paired ablations isolate the contribution of individual design choices: classifier head type (CLS vs GAP), projector output dimension, feature-loss weight, generality across three different teacher architectures (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, DeiT3-Small-21k), and standalone (no-teacher) training — this breadth strengthens confidence that the width-matching recipe itself is robust and not an artifact of a single configuration.

The proposed remedies are simple, architecture-agnostic, and easy to reproduce/implement (a single linear projector or widening one transformer block), which increases the practical value of the contribution for compact ViT design even independent of the theoretical narrative.
weaknesses: The central diagnostic tool (token-level Spectral Energy Pattern via 1D DFT along the channel axis) is mathematically questionable: channel index in a transformer's hidden dimension has no inherent notion of adjacency, periodicity, or translation invariance, so treating it as a "signal" for DFT and interpreting the result as meaningful "frequency" content is not well justified. For any vector with roughly decorrelated/exchangeable entries under an arbitrary index ordering, a unitary transform such as DFT is expected to produce an approximately flat (linear cumulative) energy spectrum purely as a generic statistical/mathematical property, independent of any genuine 'encoding' behavior specific to trained ViT representations. The paper provides no control experiments (e.g., random Gaussian vectors of matching dimension, or channel-permutation invariance checks) to rule out this trivial explanation, which is critical since the near-perfectly diagonal, near-identical SEP curves across wildly different architectures (D=192 to D=1280) are exactly what one would expect from this generic artifact rather than a genuine architecture-specific phenomenon.

The two proposed 'fixes' both increase the student's parameter count and last-layer capacity (a wider last block adds substantially more parameters/FLOPs, e.g. in its expanded FFN, and even the lightweight projector adds parameters retained at inference), yet the paper never reports parameter or FLOP counts for the modified students versus the baseline, nor compares against a natural control such as a uniformly-scaled larger DeiT-Tiny variant with matched parameter budget. This leaves unresolved whether the gains stem specifically from resolving an 'encoding mismatch' or simply from adding more capacity at the classification interface, which is a much more mundane and previously known explanation.

Novelty relative to prior work is not clearly established: retaining a projector at inference for feature alignment closely resembles ideas already explored in cited prior work on the role of projectors in KD (e.g., references [32], [33]), and the paper does not clearly delineate what is new beyond applying and characterizing these known techniques through the SVD/SEP lens.

Experimental validation of the proposed methods is essentially limited to a single student architecture (DeiT-Tiny); while multiple teachers are tested, no other compact student families, sizes, or other vision backbones (e.g., hierarchical/window-based students) are evaluated, limiting confidence in generality of the 'reactivation' claims across the broader compact ViT design space.

No comparison to existing state-of-the-art ViT-specific distillation methods (e.g., ViTKD, DIST, manifold distillation) is provided on the same student/teacher pair to contextualize whether the achieved accuracy (77.5–78.2%) is competitive with, or superior to, the current best practice, only an internal baseline (naive SpectralKD) is used for comparison.

Results appear to be single-run numbers without reported variance across seeds, which is a limitation for claims of robustness given that some reported deltas (e.g., +0.21% for naive SpectralKD, or differences among ablation rows) are within typical run-to-run noise for ImageNet training.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and logically organized, walking the reader from a global SVD analysis to a token-level diagnostic and finally to two concrete remedies.

An extensive set of SVD analyses is provided across six different ViT architectures/families (ViT-Tiny/Large/Huge, DeiT-Small, CaiT-S24, Swin-Small) in the main text and appendix, lending some generality to the 'globally low-rank' observation.
The proposed fixes (post-hoc projector retained at inference; widening only the last block) are simple, architecture-agnostic, and easy to implement.

The empirical gains on ImageNet-1K with a DeiT-Tiny student are sizeable and are shown to be robust across several ablations (classifier head type, projector width, feature-loss weight) and across three different teachers (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, DeiT3-Small-21k), which is a reasonable attempt at generality testing.
The finding that the architectural modifications also help the student when trained without any teacher (Table 7) is a useful, falsifiable prediction stemming from the paper's hypothesis.
weaknesses: The core SEP diagnostic applies a 1D DFT along the channel axis of a token's feature vector, but the channel axis has no translation-invariant or periodic structure (unlike spatial or temporal signals); channel ordering is essentially arbitrary (depends on training/init), so it is unclear that 'frequency bins' in this transform correspond to anything physically meaningful such as 'bandwidth' or 'encoding richness.' For a generic (non-sparse, non-structured) vector expressed in an arbitrary orthonormal basis unaligned with its natural sparsity directions, energy will generically spread across most DFT coefficients regardless of the underlying network — this near-diagonal SEP curve could be a near-tautological property of applying a fixed unitary transform to decorrelated/isotropic-ish vectors rather than a genuine discovery about ViT 'encoding patterns.' The paper does not rule out this alternative, much simpler explanation (e.g., via a control such as random Gaussian vectors with matched per-dimension variance, or random permutations of the channel order, which should produce a similarly diagonal curve if the hypothesis above is correct).

The central 'paradox' may be partly a straw man: using a linear projector/regressor between student and teacher feature dimensions is already common practice in CNN feature-KD literature (e.g., FitNets' regressor), so the finding that adding a projector reactivates feature-map MSE is less surprising than claimed, and the paper does not clearly justify why this has not already resolved the ViT feature-KD problem in prior works it cites as failing.

The reported gains from both strategies are confounded with increased parameter/FLOP count: widening the last block or adding a projector increases the student's capacity. The paper does not report parameter counts/FLOPs for the modified students nor compare against parameter-matched baselines (e.g., a deeper or differently-widened DeiT-Tiny without the specific 'teacher-width-matching' design) to isolate whether gains stem from the hypothesized 'encoding mismatch' resolution versus simply added capacity.

Results are reported as single numbers without variance/error bars or multiple seeds, despite several reported deltas being small (e.g., 0.1–0.3%), making it hard to assess statistical significance of some comparisons (e.g., Table 4's dimension ablation, Table 5's loss-weight ablation).

Experiments are restricted to a single student (DeiT-Tiny) and a single dataset/task (ImageNet-1K classification); no results on other compact architectures (e.g., Swin-Tiny, MobileViT) or downstream tasks (detection/segmentation), limiting evidence for the generality of the claimed architectural bottleneck and design guidance.

The comparison baseline for 'naive feature KD' is limited to a single recent method (SpectralKD); other established feature-distillation variants (e.g., FitNets-style regressor, attention transfer, ReviewKD-style strategies) are not evaluated on ViTs as baselines, making it harder to assess how much of the improvement is attributable specifically to the paper's mismatch-guided insight versus general improvements from any reasonable projector-based feature KD setup.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical narrative that connects two diagnostics (global SVD rank and token-level spectral energy) to resolve an intuitively puzzling observation (low-rank yet hard to distill) in ViT feature KD.

The proposed remedies (post-hoc linear lifting projector, native last-block width widening) are simple, lightweight, and architecture-agnostic, and they are shown to meaningfully reactivate plain MSE feature distillation, which is a practically useful finding for a problem noted as unresolved in prior work.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: ablations across classifier head type (CLS vs GAP), projector output dimension, feature-loss weight, multiple teachers (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, DeiT3-Small-21k), and a 'standalone, no-teacher' control showing the architectural change itself helps.

Good transparency on training protocol/hyperparameters, aiding reproducibility, and an extensive appendix replicating the SVD/SEP analysis across six different ViT-family architectures (ViT-Tiny/Large/Huge, Swin-Small, DeiT-Small, CaiT-S24), lending some support to claimed universality.
The paper is clearly written, with an easy-to-follow structure (SVD paradox → SEP resolution → two concrete strategies → experiments).
weaknesses: The core SEP diagnostic (1D DFT along the channel dimension) is conceptually questionable: feature channels in a ViT have no inherent topological order akin to time or space, so applying a DFT and treating bins as a 'frequency/bandwidth' measure is somewhat arbitrary. A near-diagonal cumulative energy curve is close to what one would expect from DFT of an unordered, unstructured vector with roughly flat average squared-coefficient magnitude, which raises the concern that the 'high per-token utilization' finding may be a generic artifact of unordered high-dimensional vectors rather than a specific, meaningful property of ViT encodings. The paper does not include a control (e.g., random vectors of matching norm/distribution, or permuted channel orderings) to rule this out.

The two architectural interventions substantially increase model capacity/parameters at the last layer (widening to teacher's full width, or adding a projector), and the paper does not cleanly separate 'resolving encoding mismatch by matching the teacher's specific subspace' from the more mundane explanation 'more capacity in the last layer generally improves accuracy and makes feature alignment easier.' A controlled experiment widening to a non-teacher-matched width (other than the existing 256/320/384/448 projector-dimension ablation, which already shows mixed support for the 'must match teacher exactly' claim, e.g., 320-dim outperforming 384-dim standalone) would strengthen the causal story.

No comparison against stronger, more specialized existing ViT feature-distillation methods (e.g., ViTKD, manifold distillation, ScaleKD) beyond a single SpectralKD baseline; it is unclear whether the proposed minimal fixes are competitive with, or surpass, the existing more complex literature it aims to position itself against.

Results appear to be reported from single training runs without variance/multiple seeds, and the widened-last-block strategy's added FLOPs/parameter overhead relative to the baseline student is not explicitly quantified or discussed, making it harder to judge efficiency trade-offs.

The causal framing ('this resolves the paradox', 'explains why feature-map KD fails') is somewhat stronger than the correlational evidence supports; the analysis is diagnostic/observational and the proposed fixes, while effective, do not definitively establish per-token channel-utilization mismatch as the unique causal mechanism as opposed to simple capacity bottleneck at the last layer.

strengths: Extensive and systematic empirical analysis spanning per-image SVD, dataset-level PCA, and a novel token-level Spectral Energy Pattern (SEP) diagnostic across 15+ architectures (SL, SSL, and multimodal), which lends good support to the claimed 'encoding mismatch' phenomenon and shows it is not specific to one model family.

The narrative is clear and well-motivated: it identifies an apparent paradox (per-image low-rank vs. dataset-level high-rank subspace rotation) and resolves it with a complementary spectral-bandwidth view (SEP), providing an intuitive and largely consistent explanation for why naive feature-map KD fails in ViT compression.

The proposed remedies (Lift, WideLast) are simple, minimal, and easy to implement, and the paper shows they consistently reactivate feature-map KD (even plain MSE) across multiple teachers (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, DeiT3-Small) and multiple KD combinations, with sizeable Top-1 improvements on ImageNet-1K.

Reasonably thorough ablations (classification head type, projector width, feature loss weight) and an additional standalone (no-teacher) experiment that isolates the architectural bottleneck from the distillation signal itself, strengthening the causal interpretation.

Reproducibility appears reasonable: equations for all diagnostics are precisely defined, training protocol (optimizer, schedule, epochs, hardware) is specified, and the authors state code/raw data will be released.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against existing alignment-based ViT distillation methods explicitly designed to bridge width mismatches (e.g., ScaleKD, VkD, OFA-KD), despite these being discussed at length in related work; without such baselines it is hard to judge whether Lift/WideLast are competitive with, or merely simpler than, the state of the art.

The core fixes (adding a wider projector at the end, or widening the last block) are conceptually straightforward and have partial precedent in prior projector-based KD works; the paper's novelty rests mainly on the diagnostic framing rather than a fundamentally new remedy, somewhat limiting originality of the solution itself (though the analysis is more novel).

WideLast increases the student's parameter count/FLOPs at the last block to match the teacher width, and Lift adds a linear projector retained at inference — the paper does not report the resulting parameter/FLOPs overhead relative to the base DeiT-Tiny, which is important for judging whether the 'compression' framing and comparisons to baseline compact models remain fair.

Main ImageNet-1K results (Table 2, 6, 7) appear to be single-run numbers with no reported variance across seeds, making it difficult to assess whether the reported gains (some as small as ~0.5-1%) are statistically robust.

The analysis is restricted to the last layer/endpoint; the paper acknowledges but does not empirically explore whether the same encoding-mismatch account extends to intermediate-layer feature distillation, which is common in practice and where feature KD sometimes succeeds even in compression.

The causal chain linking subspace rotation and SEP bandwidth specifically to KD training failure (as opposed to, e.g., generic optimization or gradient-conflict effects between CE and feature losses) is inferred from correlational analysis and architectural fixes rather than demonstrated with a more controlled/mechanistic experiment (e.g., directly measuring feature-loss vs. accuracy correlation, or ablating rotation vs. bandwidth independently).

strengths: The paper provides an extensive empirical characterization (sample-wise SVD, dataset-level PCA, and the proposed SEP diagnostic) across a wide range of architectures and training regimes (SL, SSL, multimodal), which is a nontrivial amount of experimental work and gives the reader a comprehensive empirical picture (Table 1, Appendix B/C).

The proposed remedies (Lift and WideLast) are simple, easy to implement, and the paper runs a reasonably thorough set of ablations (classifier head type, projector width, feature-loss weight) that probe robustness of the claimed mechanism.

The paper tests generality across more than one teacher (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, DeiT3-Small-21k) and shows the architectural fix also helps the standalone (non-distilled) student, which is a nice internal consistency check supporting the 'architectural bottleneck' narrative.
The writing is generally clear, and the narrative connecting per-image SVD, dataset PCA, and SEP into a single 'encoding mismatch' story is conceptually tidy and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The dataset-level PCA and SVD computations use the uncentered second moment / raw feature matrices (Eq. 4, Eq. 1-3). This raises a serious methodological concern: a large fraction of the 'required dimension' at the dataset level could simply reflect a shared mean/offset direction (e.g., LayerNorm affine bias, common channel-wise DC component) rather than genuine per-image subspace rotation. Without a centered-PCA control/ablation, the central claim of 'dataset-level non-low-rankness due to subspace rotation' is not clearly distinguished from a much more mundane artifact of not removing the mean, which would substantially weaken the paper's main diagnostic claim.

The SEP analysis applies a 1D DFT along the channel dimension, but channels in a ViT embedding have no inherent ordering or frequency structure (unlike a spatial or temporal signal). For a sufficiently generic/incoherent vector expressed in a fixed orthogonal basis unrelated to its true 'informative' directions, one would expect an approximately uniform (hence near-diagonal) energy spread almost by default (Parseval's theorem applied to a basis with no special alignment to the signal). The paper does not rule out that the observed 'architecture-invariant encoding law' is simply this generic phenomenon rather than a deep and novel discovery about token encoding; a control using random orthogonal bases or a permuted-channel ordering is needed to make this claim convincing.

WideLast, the strongest-performing fix, enlarges the final Transformer block to the teacher's width (e.g., 384 vs. 192 for DeiT-Tiny), which substantially increases parameters/FLOPs near the output. The paper never reports parameter counts or FLOPs for Lift/WideLast variants versus the baseline student or teacher, making it impossible to judge whether the reported accuracy gains are due to resolving a genuine 'architectural bottleneck' versus simply adding meaningful extra capacity/compute, which would undercut the compression-efficiency motivation framed in the introduction.

The practical remedies (retaining a linear projector at inference to match teacher width, or widening the last block) are conceptually similar to long-standing projector-based distillation practices (e.g., FitNets-style regressors, several of the cited projector/alignment works in Appendix A.3). The paper does not clearly establish that these fixes outperform or substantially differ from existing projector-based or alignment-based ViT-KD methods (ScaleKD, VkD, OFA-KD, MiniViT, etc.) in a head-to-head comparison; results are only benchmarked against the authors' own 'naive feature KD' baseline, not against published state-of-the-art DeiT-Tiny distillation numbers from the literature, limiting the demonstrated significance of the contribution.

All main experiments use a single compact student (DeiT-Tiny) on ImageNet-1K; no results are shown on other downstream tasks (detection/segmentation) or other student scales, despite the conclusion explicitly flagging this as future work. This limits the generality of the claimed 'architecture-invariant encoding law' as a practically useful phenomenon beyond the one architecture pair studied in depth.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the ImageNet-1K training runs, despite several reported deltas being small (e.g., +0.21%, +0.55%, +0.68%), making it hard to assess whether some of the finer-grained ablation conclusions (e.g., projector dimension sweep in Table 4, head-type ablation in Table 3) are statistically meaningful rather than noise from single training runs.

Some values in Table 1 and the appendix PCA figures appear unstable (e.g., very low per-image/dataset dimensions required for 80% energy such as '1' for several SSL/MAE models), which is consistent with the centering/mean-offset concern above and suggests the PCA-based diagnostic pipeline may need additional validation or sanity checks before being used as the primary evidence for the paper's central claims.

strengths: The three-way diagnostic (per-image SVD, dataset-level shared-subspace PCA, and token-level Spectral Energy Pattern) is a clear and intuitive framework that resolves an apparent paradox (per-image low rank vs. difficulty of narrow-student feature matching) with concrete, well-visualized evidence.

The 'architecture-invariant encoding law' observed via SEP is validated across an unusually broad set of 15 models spanning supervised, self-supervised (DINO/DINOv2/MAE), and multimodal (CLIP) training regimes, lending credibility to the claim of a general phenomenon rather than a CaiT-specific artifact.

The proposed fixes (Lift and WideLast) are simple, minimal, and easy to reproduce, and the paper provides thorough ablations (classifier head type, projector width, feature-loss weight) that show the improvements are not fragile to these design choices.

Testing generality across multiple teacher architectures (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, DeiT3-Small-21k) and showing gains even without any teacher (standalone training) strengthens the causal story that the identified bottleneck is architectural rather than an artifact of the distillation pipeline.
The paper is clearly written, with results tied back to the motivating analysis in a coherent narrative, and raw data/code are stated to be provided.
weaknesses: The central remedies both add parameters/FLOPs to the student at the last layer (WideLast in particular substantially increases attention/MLP parameters in the final block), but the paper never isolates whether gains stem from the specific 'encoding mismatch' fix or simply from added capacity; a controlled comparison against alternative ways of adding equivalent capacity (e.g., widening an earlier block, adding equal extra parameters elsewhere) is missing and would be needed to support the specific mechanistic claim.

Despite extensive related-work discussion of existing projector-based/alignment-based ViT distillation methods (ScaleKD, VkD, OFA-KD, ViTKD) that already use learned projectors or alignment modules, the paper does not empirically benchmark Lift/WideLast against these methods on the same student-teacher pair, making it hard to assess whether the proposed remedies are actually more effective or just a simpler re-derivation of known tricks.

All main experiments use a single student architecture (DeiT-Tiny) and a single dataset (ImageNet-1K); it is unclear whether the diagnosed mismatch and fixes generalize to other compression ratios, student families (e.g., hierarchical/CNN-hybrid), or tasks beyond classification.

The use of a 1D DFT along the channel dimension to define SEP is not well justified conceptually, since channel ordering in a ViT is largely arbitrary/unstructured (unlike a spatial or temporal signal where frequency has physical meaning); the paper does not discuss whether the 'spectral universality' result would hold under other orthogonal bases/permutations, which affects the interpretability of the 'high-bandwidth' claim as a genuine encoding property versus a generic property of high-dimensional near-isotropic vectors.

Results are reported as single-run top-1 accuracies without variance across seeds, making it difficult to judge whether some of the smaller deltas (e.g., +0.21% for naive SpectralKD, or differences between Lift/WideLast variants) are statistically meaningful.
